strengths: The task is well motivated: editing images using a target emotion alone could benefit affective computing and controllable image generation. The examples demonstrate semantic modifications beyond conventional color and style transfer.

EmoPair is a potentially useful resource, combining 331,595 automatically annotated InstructPix2Pix pairs with 6,949 additionally generated pairs. The manuscript attributes its underlying datasets and models and describes the curation pipeline.

The human evaluation provides evidence beyond classifier scores. Figure 5 reports an average 56% preference for EmoEditor, and the supplement includes a laboratory study and informative breakdowns by emotion direction.

Extensive visual examples, explicit failure cases, and discussion of manipulation risks improve transparency. The manuscript also reports informed consent, institutional review approval, and participant compensation.
weaknesses: The supervised training objective is inadequately specified (Sec. 3.2). The manuscript defines z=E(Is), adds noise to this source-image latent, and predicts that noise while conditioning on the same source latent. The paired target image never enters the stated objective. Implemented literally, this supervises source reconstruction rather than the desired editing transformation. This may be a notation error, but the actual objective must be clarified to establish technical soundness.

The automatic evaluation is strongly coupled to the method: the same predictor P supplies dataset labels and filtering, selects outputs during inference, and computes EMR, ESR, and ENRD. Removing the inference critic reduces EMR from 50.20% to 5.06% (Table 1), making independent validation particularly important. Baselines are not given comparable classifier-based selection over up to 20 editing rounds. Independent evaluators, human ablations, and comparisons using equivalent inference budgets are needed to isolate the contribution.

ESR is mathematically problematic as defined in Sec. 4. Under the conventional interpretation, KL(e_g || e_oh) is infinite whenever the generated distribution assigns probability to a non-target class, because e_oh is exactly one-hot. The manuscript specifies neither smoothing nor a reversed divergence convention, so the reported ESR values cannot be reproduced from its definition.

The architectural and reasoning claims exceed the demonstrated novelty. The global embedding depends only on the target emotion, giving the same embedding for every source image with that target; its cosine alignment cannot itself represent source-specific editing instructions. The image-conditioning branch largely follows the pretrained InstructPix2Pix framework. There are no architecture or data-matched fine-tuning comparisons to isolate these claims. The closely related Affective Image Filter is cited but not evaluated, while direct InstructPix2Pix receives unusually weak one-word prompts.

Human evidence supports a modest, variable advantage rather than consistent superiority. Preference against LMS is 54% online and 49% in the laboratory study (Fig. S6). Confidence intervals and analyses accounting for repeated participants and images are absent. Only 27% of online participants pass screening, making transparent reporting of retained samples and filtering sensitivity important. The reported 417,000 trials also conflicts with 417 participants completing 100 trials; this arithmetic correction is secondary to the statistical concerns.

The central requirement of preserving scene semantics is insufficiently evaluated. Human trials assess emotion alone, and pixel/edge differences do not establish semantic preservation. Figure 6 includes substantial replacements, such as a cross monument becoming the Eiffel Tower. Table 1 also shows that both ablations improve ENRD and ESS, contrary to the accompanying claim that removing components worsens these measures. Quantitative evaluation covers cross-valence edits; fine-grained within-valence editing and neutral-image generalization receive only qualitative examples.

Dataset reliability and reproducibility remain uncertain. Most pairs receive labels from a predictor with 73% accuracy on EmoSet, without an independent human audit on the synthetic paired images or an ablation separating EPAS and EPGS. Descriptions of supervision as human-annotated need reconciliation with the automated curation pipeline. Essential details—including learning rate, batch size, training duration, emotion-encoder dimensions, and inference guidance settings—are missing.
